strengths: Novel theoretical characterization: Elegant connection between Schur-convexity/concavity of reward aggregators and heterogeneity gain is original and insightful, reducing to simple convexity tests for broad aggregator families

Well-executed experimental validation: Comprehensive experiments from matrix games to embodied navigation systematically validate theory; rediscovery of predictions by HED in complex environments is convincing
Solid algorithmic contribution: HED's direct gradient backpropagation through differentiable simulators is more efficient than RL-based alternatives; algorithm is well-motivated and implemented
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Paper is well-written with clear motivation; code, hyperparameters, and computational resources provided for reproducibility
Connects to multiple domains: Shows applicability across matrix games, Colonel Blotto, level-based foraging, and navigation tasks, demonstrating some generality within task allocation framework
weaknesses: Severely limited theoretical scope: Theory applies only to separable tasks with factorizable rewards (inner aggregator over agents, outer over tasks); cannot handle inseparable rewards, task interactions, or constraints common in practice. Cannot analyze state transition dynamics' effect on heterogeneity

Critical theory-practice gap: Theorems characterize when heterogeneity CAN help, but paper acknowledges ∆R > 0 is only 'evidence' not 'formal guarantee' that agents will learn to exploit it. Multi-Goal-Capture empirically shows gains smaller than theory predicts, and negative gains occur due to learning dynamics

Questionable practical significance: Figure 4b shows heterogeneity gain vanishes with richer observations—homogeneous agents achieve behavioral diversity through behavioral typing even with shared policies, undermining the practical advantage of structural heterogeneity

HED algorithm limitations: Requires differentiable simulation (limiting applicability); high variance in parameter learning (Fig. 5); no convergence guarantees; design choices (training regime timing) unjustified; primarily demonstrated on small scale (N=M≤4)

Incomplete experimental evaluation: No comparison with heterogeneity-promoting baselines (ROMA, RODE, HyperMARL, etc.) or other environment design methods; only informal PAIRED comparison; circular validation in matrix games; missing ablations on HED components and hyperparameter sensitivity

strengths: Clean theoretical characterization: Theorems 3.1-3.3 elegantly connect Schur-convexity/concavity of aggregation operators to heterogeneity gains, providing clear and actionable conditions for when behavioral diversity is beneficial.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Rigorous progression from matrix games (exact theoretical predictions) to embodied environments (tag, football, multi-goal-capture) demonstrates theory transfer with appropriate controls and multiple random seeds.
Practical relevance: Addresses genuine MARL trade-off (neural heterogeneity vs. learning efficiency) and provides concrete reward design guidance valuable to practitioners.

Well-structured presentation and broad applicability: Clear progression from theory to algorithm to experiments; framework unifies diverse existing environments (Colonel Blotto, Level-Based Foraging) through task-allocation abstraction.

Methodological rigor and reproducibility: Extensive appendices with full proofs, implementation details, configuration files; code provided; distinction between neural and behavioral heterogeneity clearly articulated.
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: Theory analyzes instantaneous single-shot rewards while experiments involve time-extended learning; negative empirical ΔR values (e.g., Table 9: -0.75±0.5) for theoretically predicted ΔR=0 cases suggest learning dynamics fundamentally violate assumptions. Paper acknowledges but doesn't resolve this, undermining practical utility.

Observability trade-off severely limits applicability: Appendix N shows empirical heterogeneity gain vanishes as agent observability increases (neurally homogeneous agents become behaviorally heterogeneous through observation conditioning). This crucial limitation contradicts applicability claims and should be in main text.

Restrictive theoretical scope and assumptions: (i) Framework limited to task-allocation domains only; cannot address multi-robot manipulation or other non-effort-allocation problems. (ii) Theorem 3.3 requires constant-sum task scores assumption with limited discussion of when it holds. (iii) Theory predicts *when* heterogeneity helps, not whether learning algorithms discover solutions.

Limited algorithmic novelty and HetGPS limitations: HetGPS is primarily a validation tool with no convergence guarantees (acknowledged in App. P.2). Requires differentiable simulator, limiting real-world applicability. 25% training overhead non-trivial for large-scale problems. Relationship to PAIRED suggests incremental novelty.

Problematic scaling behavior: N=M=8 results (Table 9) show negative ΔR values persist due to neurally heterogeneous agents requiring more learning time, suggesting theory doesn't capture important learning dynamics. This practical limitation is downplayed despite contradicting claims of practical utility.

Incremental theoretical contribution: Schur-convexity is well-established; Theorems 3.1-3.3 follow straightforwardly from existing majorization theory. Primary contribution is application to task-allocation domains, which is valuable but somewhat incremental compared to foundational MARL work.

Incomplete analysis of learning dynamics: No formal characterization of when agents will discover heterogeneous solutions or converge to theoretically optimal allocations. Gap between optimal allocations (theory) and empirically learned policies (practice) not adequately addressed.
